senses.gloss:
kuśāsana
(‘seat of कुश grass’)
------------------------------------------
For a good meditation, a conducive external atmosphere is as much necessary as internal conditions like the health of the body and a peaceful मिन्द्.
A level and clean place, away from all sources of noise and disturbance is a must. (vide Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10). Sitting posture is the most comfortable one (vide the Brahmasūtras 4.1.17). For this, a good seat is necessary.
The Bhagavadgītā (6.11) recommends a seat comprising the कुश grass, the deerskin and a cotton cloth spread one over the other in that order. The first one is called कुशासन, a seat made of कुश grass (Poa cynosuroides).
Now-a-days, kuśāsanas made of कुश grass woven like a small mat, are available in the market.
Since the कुश grass is considered holy and is closely associated with religious rites and ceremonies, the कुशासन is recommended for meditation as also in the religious ceremonies.

Kūṣmāṇḍahoma
(‘oblations [into the fire to offset the evils of] sins’)
------------------------------------------
Man is prone to committing sins (See PĀTAKA for details.) knowingly or unknowingly. When he realises it and repents for it he may think of some ways and means of offsetting their consequences. Such means are called prāyaścittas. The कूष्माण्डहोम is one such, of Vedic origin.
Oblations of आज्य (ghee) are offered into a duly consecrated fire with the 53 mantras (forming the praśnas [sections] 3, 4, 5, and 6 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka) known as Kūṣmāṇḍa-mantras. अग्नि, the fire-god, is the deity to whom prayers are addressed and offerings are made.
Out of the several sins expressly mentioned here, a few may be cited: killing an embryo; prohibited sexual relationships; telling lies; humiliating others out of arrogance; cheating; violence against one’s own parents; damaging nature; secretly committed sins and so on.
The person who wants to perform this होम can do it himself directly or through a competent priest. Shaving the head, ड़स्तिन्ग्, not consuming meat, observing celibacy, sleeping on the ground—these are the disciplines to be observed before performing it. This is called ‘dīkṣā’. This दीक्षा may be observed from one year up to three days prior to the performance of the होम.
The कूष्माण्डहोम has to be performed at the beginning of every rite that involves a होम such as पुṁसवन, चूडाकरण, उपनयन and विवाह. (See under each title for details.) It has to be done before the performance of other homas also, like Gaṇapathi-होम and Rudrahoma.

Kuśa
------------------------------------------
As per the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa of Vāmīki (chs. 91, 98 and 108), कुश and लव, the twins were born of सीता in the hermitage of वाल्मीकि. सीता was pregnant when she had been banished by राम, being afraid of the calumny that had spread in his kingdom, though both of them were innocent and pure. सीता had then been sheltered by the sage वाल्मीकि in his hermitage.
Kuśa and लव were educated by वाल्मीकि in the various arts and sciences. He had also taught them to sing the whole of Rāmāyaṇa to the accompaniment of musical instruments. The boys who attended the अश्वमेध sacrifice, along with वाल्मीकि, endeared themselves to one and all by their enchanting मुसिच् and charming appearance. After revealing the truth, वाल्मीकि handed over सीता and the two boys to राम. सीता, however, was absorbed into the bowels of the earth by Bhūmātā (Mother Earth) at her request.
Later, राम coronated कुश as the king of Kuśāvatī near the Vindhyā mountains and लव at Śrāvasti before exiting from this world. कुश, later on, shifted his capital to अयोध्या.
Kuśa had two wives, Campakā and Kumudvatī. His lineage continued through the eight sons of the latter.
The word कुश also stands for the कुश grass (same as दर्भ) (Poa cynosuroides) used in religious rites and the island Kuśadvīpa, one among the seven described in Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्.
